pages.text:
*Ama's Stall Ledger, Night 57. Bowls sold: 34. Lanterns made: 112. Volunteers: everyone.*

The bell above the office door was still ringing when I burst through. Ms. Wu was sharpening a pencil, her bun tight and neat. I explained the whole plan in one breath: hundreds of lanterns, stories, games, and a trail of riddles. We needed Ms. Xu, the city inspector, to see that the lane was more than just stalls. It was a living thing.

Ms. Wu stopped sharpening. She looked at me, then at the empty classroom, and finally at the cupboard by the door.

"I have wanted to do this for three years," she said. Her voice was quiet but firm. She opened the cupboard. Inside, stacked neatly like a pile of math textbooks, was a bag of bamboo strips. She pulled them out with a heavy thud. "I was waiting for someone to ask."

I stared at the bamboo. It smelled faintly of dried grass and sun. "We can start now," I said.

"We will need paper," Ms. Wu said, turning to the whiteboard. "And glue. And you will need to be very quiet while I explain how to bend the wood without snapping it."

I nodded, my hands shaking a little from the cold. We had one night to build a dream, and we had the materials.
pages.image: A warm classroom scene with a small girl in a green jacket standing before a teacher, both looking at a large bag of bamboo strips on a desk, surrounded by sunlight and quiet anticipation. All shop signs, banners and hanging boards are smooth plain solid-color cloth.

pages.text:
The room turned into a workshop. Bamboo clicked and crunched under our fingers. We dipped strips in water to make them soft, then bent them into squares and circles. The air smelled of wet wood and sweet glue.

Jun sat at the back, his spiky hair sticking out in every direction. He was building a rooster. Or, at least, he said it was a rooster. It had a long, drooping neck and a crest that looked like it had given up on life.

"It’s a chicken who has met a tragedy," Hui-Ting whispered to me.

Jun looked up, his face bright with delight. "Exactly," he said. "It’s a chicken who has seen the dark side of the oyster omelet."

Yi-Chen stood by the window for a long time, watching us fumble with the paper. She wore her pink puffy vest, which was already getting sticky at the elbows. Finally, she stepped into the circle of desks.

"I can draw the designs," she said softly. Her voice was small but clear.

She took a stack of paper and began to sketch. Dragon scales, flowing ribbons, stars. When she held up the first drawing, the class went silent. It was beautiful. It was perfect.
pages.image: A group of children in a classroom crafting lanterns, with a tall boy proudly holding a lopsided paper rooster and a girl in a pink vest carefully drawing intricate patterns on white paper.

pages.text:
By the next night, the lane had transformed. Uncle Feng stood on a stool, hanging a golden omelet lantern the size of a bicycle wheel. "It’s a symbol!" he shouted. "Of our golden, crispy future!"

Old Mr. Gao, his straw hat tilted back, was testing his shrimp lantern. He hung it over the fishing pond. "Now," he said, adjusting his spectacles, "who wants to hear the riddle? Why did the shrimp cross the road?"

No one answered.

"Because the fish were swimming the other way!" he announced. The crowd of children burst into laughter, even as they tried to solve the next one.

Auntie Ping emerged from her tea stall. She held a small, elegant lantern. "I will run a Lantern Tea tent," she said. She did not mention the mall. She did not mention the empty tables. She just smiled, her glittery nails clicking against the paper.

Mr. Tsai, in his cardigan, handed me a small bundle of spices. "For the light," he said. "So the air smells like home."
pages.image: A lively night market scene where a large golden paper omelet lantern hangs above a fishing pond, with a man in a straw hat and a woman with glittery nails smiling nearby.

pages.text:
Ms. Wu handed out small tags of red paper and string. "Write a wish," she said. "Something you hope for. Tie it to the string."

I pulled a tag from my pocket. It was the one I had used to write the temple keeper’s message. My pencil felt heavy. I thought about Ama’s wrist. I thought about the shame I had felt. I thought about the smell of star anise that was not a smell, but a feeling.

I wrote: I want to be proud, out loud.

I walked to the end of the lane, where the temple tree stood. Its branches were heavy with other wishes, fluttering in the cold wind. I tied my tag to a low branch. It sat there, bright red against the dark leaves.

It did not feel like a secret anymore. It felt like a promise.

I turned back to the lane. The lights were starting to glow, casting long, warm shadows. The lane was no longer empty. It was full of light.
pages.image: A small girl in a green jacket tying a red paper tag to the branch of a large tree under the night sky, with glowing lanterns visible in the background.

pages.text:
Yi-Chen was packing her bag, her pink vest now covered in specks of white paper and glue. She looked at the lanterns, then at me.

"Can I help?" she asked. "With the stall?"

I looked at her. She had been so careful, so precise. I had been so messy, so loud.

"Can you carry bowls?" I asked.

"I have never carried a bowl in my life," she said.

I brought a bowl from the counter. It was hot, filled with the clear broth Ama had made that afternoon. I placed it in her hands.

She held it with both hands, like it was made of glass. Like it was a treasure. She did not spill a drop. She looked at me, and her eyes were bright.

"Okay," I said. "Let’s go."

We walked toward the stall, the lanterns glowing above us, the lane humming with the sound of a hundred small lights.
pages.image: A girl in a pink vest holding a steaming bowl with both hands, looking at a smaller girl in a green jacket, with warm lantern light illuminating their faces.
